title: Deadly Drone Wave Hits Kyiv, Including a Historic Science Academy
summary: A drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, as Russia carried out one of its most persistent drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital since the war began. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said nine people were killed and more than 80 injured in strikes across the country. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 24 people were hurt in the capital, six of whom were being treated in hospital. In Zaporizhzhia, an attack on infrastructure injured 32 people, and one person was killed at a logistics office in Synelnykove, southeast of Dnipro, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said 19 people had been injured in a daytime attack on a business centre in Dnipro. Officials reported strikes on a pharmaceutical company, petrol stations and a medical facility in Kyiv, as well as civilian facilities, businesses and communications infrastructure in other regions. Ukraine is struggling to counter Russia's newer jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than older propeller models. Zelenskyy said 90 of the 120 drones fired at Ukraine were jet-propelled, and the interception rate was 57 per cent. "New interceptors are being actively tested," he said, adding that some units already use them but that more work is needed to reach full effectiveness. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of deliberately targeting a scientific institution during the working day and urged allies to supply more air defences. Zelenskyy also cited a report from Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence saying Russia had launched a new wave of military mobilization. He said 8,000 North Korean troops remain in Russia, with 10,000 more being trained. Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed any notion of a new mobilization as "utter nonsense."
why_it_matters: This attack shows how modern wars are fought as much with technology as with soldiers: a faster drone can outrun a defence system, and the side that adapts quickest gains an edge. It also shows why a war in one country pulls in others, from North Korean troops to Western air-defence supplies.

background_read: Kyiv (the capital of Ukraine, a country in Eastern Europe) has been a target of Russian drone and missile strikes since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the city's air defences have become one of the most heavily tested systems of the war.

The National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine is the country's main scientific research body, founded more than a hundred years ago; striking such an institution matters because research academies train scientists and preserve a nation's knowledge.

Russia has relied heavily on long-range drones in this war. Early models were slower, propeller-driven craft; the newer jet-powered drones described in the article fly faster and higher, which makes them much harder for air defences to shoot down.

North Korea (officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, a heavily sanctioned state that has aligned itself with Moscow) has sent troops to fight alongside Russian forces — a step that widened the war's international footprint.

Air defence works by detecting incoming objects and firing interceptors at them, so a low interception rate means many drones get through; Ukraine has asked its allies for more of these systems throughout the war.

perspectives.description: For Ukraine and its partners, the response is a reason for resolve: officials say new interceptors are already in the hands of some units and are being actively tested, and outrage over a strike on a scientific institution could speed up deliveries of air-defence systems. Every drone shot down, they argue, saves civilian lives.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — those pointing to the gaps
perspectives.description: Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accuses Russia of deliberately hitting a research academy during the working day, which critics call a strategy aimed at civilian and scientific targets rather than military ones. Others warn that Western air defences are arriving too slowly, given that only 57 per cent of the drones were stopped.

The war has become a contest of constant adaptation: Russia moved from slower propeller drones to jet-powered models that fly faster and higher, while Ukraine scrambles to field new interceptors. A 57 per cent interception rate illustrates how quickly a defender's advantage can erode when the attacker upgrades.

The immediate questions are whether allies will supply enough interceptors and whether Ukraine can raise its interception rate before the next wave. Beyond that, reports of a new Russian mobilization and more North Korean troops — both denied by President Putin — suggest the war could widen further rather than wind down.
